title: Optimizing quantum error correction through error attribution
abstract: Logical error rate is a standard benchmark for quantum error correction, providing an aggregate measure of the overall effect of physical noise. In actual QEC architectures, errors at different circuit locations can have markedly different effects on logical failure even when their probabilities are equal. Here we introduce an error attribution scheme to quantitatively characterize the influence of individual circuit components on the logical error rate and use this refined information to guide targeted intervention and design for improved QEC performance. Our attribution estimator computes all component sensitivities jointly from the same Monte Carlo samples used to estimate the logical error rate. The resulting sensitivity maps identify hotspots where targeted noise reduction can most effectively improve logical performance. We test the scheme in circuit simulations of rotated surface code memories and high-rate lifted product codes: halving the noise strength on about 5\%-7\% of physical components selected by sensitivity reduces logical error rates by approximately 15\%-25\%, roughly twice the mean reduction from the same intervention on an equal number of randomly selected components. By connecting performance benchmarking to targeted optimization, our scheme provides a practical strategy for improving quantum error correction with limited resources.
summary: This paper introduces an error attribution scheme to diagnose which physical noise sources most critically impact the logical error rate in quantum error correction codes. By quantifying the sensitivity of the logical failure rate to individual noise components, the authors identify 'hotspots' in the error circuit. Targeting noise reduction efforts on these few critical components yields substantial, non-trivial improvements in QEC performance compared to random efforts.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of using the aggregate logical error rate in Quantum Error Correction (QEC) by developing a method to pinpoint which specific physical noise components contribute most significantly to overall failure.
main_result: Targeted noise reduction on the top 5%-7% of most sensitive physical components can reduce the logical error rate by 14%-25%, significantly outperforming interventions on the same number of randomly selected components.
method: An error attribution scheme is introduced to calculate the sensitivity of the logical error rate to individual noise strengths, using joint estimation from Monte Carlo samples to identify 'hotspots' in the error circuit.
model_or_system: The study applies this framework to simulate QEC circuits, specifically using rotated surface codes and high-rate lifted product codes, which are modeled under a stochastic error framework.
key_observables: Logical error rate (P_L), component sensitivities (S_alpha), and linearized marginal risk (R_alpha).
important_parameters: Noise strengths (lambda), code distances (d=3, 5, 7), and the fraction of components targeted for intervention (e.g., 5%-7%).
main_assumptions: The method assumes mutual independence of elementary noise components and relies on a linearized approximation of the marginal risk.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the error attribution framework, showing sensitivity maps that highlight 'hotspots' (critical components) and comparing the reduction in P_L achieved by targeting these hotspots versus random selection.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the error attribution framework and its estimators. It then applies this to surface codes, demonstrating that hotspots are pronounced. Finally, it quantifies the performance gains by comparing targeted intervention against random intervention across various code sizes.
why_interesting: This work provides a practical, data-driven optimization tool for QEC hardware design, moving beyond simple benchmarking to guide resource allocation for maximum performance gain.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Fig. 3 shows the comparison results. Relative to the circuit without intervention, the hotspot-guided intervention reduces the logical error rates by 14.35%, 14.92%, and 17.57% for d = 3, 5, 7, respectively. For comparison, applying the same intervention to the same number of physical components se- lected uniformly at random reduces the logical error rates by 7.34%, 7.84%, and 10.84% on average for d = 3, 5, 7, respec- tively. Figure 4. Relative logical error rate reduction versus intervention budget. The d = 7 rotated surface code circuit contains 265 physical components and uses seven syndrome rounds at p = 0.001. Orange circles show the reduction from hotspot-guided intervention, while blue squares show the mean reduction from random intervention over 40 sets of k components chosen uniformly at random. The local error rate of each selected component is reduced by a fraction α = 0.5. Error bars indicate 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
